claim: Streptococcus pneumoniae kills over a million individuals each year, despite the introduction of several vaccines targeting its capsule.
source: The opportunistic human pathogen Streptococcus pneumoniae (the pneumococcus) kills over a million individuals each year, despite the introduction of several vaccines targeting its capsule (Croucher et al., 2018; O'Brien et al., 2009; Prina et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Croucher et al., 2018; O'Brien et al., 2009; Prina et al., 2015).

claim: Genes associated with capsule biosynthesis are rapidly transferred from one pneumococcal strain to another by competence activation, contributing to vaccine escape.
source: Because of its ability to take-up DNA from its environment by competence activation, genes associated with capsule biosynthesis are rapidly transferred from one strain to the other thereby contributing to vaccine escape (Salvadori et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Salvadori et al., 2019).

claim: Competence-dependent recombination plays an important role in the spread of antibiotic resistance in S. pneumoniae.
source: In addition, antibiotic resistance remains a cause of concern and competence-dependent recombination plays an important role in the spread of drug resistance (Sw et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Sw et al., 2019).

claim: One of the main genetic sources for penicillin resistance in S. pneumoniae is DNA acquired from non-pathogenic Streptococci from the viridans group such as S. mitis.
source: For example, one of the main genetic sources for penicillin resistance in S. pneumoniae is DNA acquired from non-pathogenic Streptococci from the viridans group such as S. mitis that also lives in the human nasal and oral cavities (Bryskier, 2002; Janoir et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bryskier, 2002; Janoir et al., 1999).

claim: Antibiotic-resistant pneumococci and vaccine-escape variants remain an important cause of invasive infections despite the introduction of conjugate vaccines.
source: Consistently, antibiotic- resistant pneumococci and vaccine-escape variants remain an important cause of invasive infections in spite of the introduction of the conjugate vaccines (Fenoll et al., 2018; Levy et al., 2019; Ouldali et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Fenoll et al., 2018; Levy et al., 2019; Ouldali et al., 2018).

claim: Horizontal gene transfer via natural transformation is present in many human pathogens where it promotes the spread of virulence determinants and antibiotic resistance.
source: Importantly, horizontal gene transfer (HGT) via natural transformation is not only conserved in Streptococci but is present in many human pathogens where it promotes the spread of virulence determinants and antibiotic resistance (Brockhurst et al., 2019; Dubnau and Blokesch, 2019; Johnston et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Brockhurst et al., 2019; Dubnau and Blokesch, 2019; Johnston et al., 2014).

claim: In contrast to many other competent pathogens such as Acinetobacter spp. and Neisseria meningitidis in which competence is constitutively expressed, competence development in S. pneumoniae is only activated under specific conditions.
source: In contrast to many other competent pathogens such as Acinetobacter spp. and Neisseria meningitidis in which competence is constitutively expressed, competence development in S. pneumoniae is only activated under specific conditions (Blokesch, 2016; Claverys et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Blokesch, 2016; Claverys et al., 2006).

claim: Pneumococcal competence is under control of a two-component quorum sensing system.
source: Pneumococcal competence is under control of a two-component quorum sensing system (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 which shows the quorum sensing system components.

claim: ComC is cleaved and exported by the peptidase-containing ATP-binding cassette transporter ComAB.
source: ComC is cleaved and exported by the peptidase-containing ATP-binding cassette transporter ComAB (Chandler and Morrison, 1988; Håvarstein et al., 1995; Hui et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Chandler and Morrison, 1988; Håvarstein et al., 1995; Hui et al., 1995).

claim: Cleaved ComC autoinducer is commonly referred to as competence stimulating peptide (CSP).
source: Cleaved ComC autoinducer is commonly referred to as competence stimulating peptide (CSP) (Alloing et al., 1996; Håvarstein et al., 1996; Håvarstein et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Alloing et al., 1996; Håvarstein et al., 1996; Håvarstein et al., 1995).

claim: CSP is recognized by the membrane-bound histidine kinase ComD.
source: CSP is recognized by the membrane-bound histidine kinase ComD (Håvarstein et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Håvarstein et al., 1996).

claim: Once a certain threshold level of CSP has been reached, ComD will autophosphorylate and transfer the phosphoryl group to the response regulator ComE.
source: Once a certain threshold level of CSP has been reached, as the culture reaches higher densities, or when other environmental factors increase local CSP concentrations (Domenech et al., 2018; Moreno-Gámez et al., 2017), ComD will autophosphorylate and transfer the phosphoryl group to the response regulator ComE (Martin et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Domenech et al., 2018; Moreno-Gámez et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2013).

claim: Phosphorylated ComE dimerizes and binds to a specific DNA sequence.
source: Phosphorylated ComE then dimerizes (Boudes et al., 2014; Sanchez et al., 2015) and binds to a specific DNA sequence (Martin et al., 2013; Pestova et al., 1996; Slager et al., 2019; Ween et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Boudes et al., 2014; Sanchez et al., 2015; Martin et al., 2013; Pestova et al., 1996; Slager et al., 2019; Ween et al., 1999).

claim: The comCDE and comAB operons are under direct control of ComE, setting up a positive feedback loop.
source: The comCDE and comAB operons are under direct control of ComE, setting up a positive feedback loop.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of the competence regulatory system.

claim: Phosphorylated ComE activates expression of the gene encoding the alternative sigma factor ComX.
source: Importantly, phosphorylated ComE also activates expression of the gene encoding the alternative sigma factor ComX.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of the competence regulatory system.

claim: ComX activates transcription of the late com genes, which includes the genes required for DNA uptake and integration.
source: ComX activates transcription of the so-called late com genes, which includes the genes required for DNA uptake and integration (Campbell et al., 1998; Dagkessamanskaia et al., 2004; Luo et al., 2003; Pestova and Morrison, 1998; Slager et al., 2019; Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Campbell et al., 1998; Dagkessamanskaia et al., 2004; Luo et al., 2003; Pestova and Morrison, 1998; Slager et al., 2019) and reference to Figure 1.

claim: While regulation of competence is highly diverse between naturally transformable bacteria, the actual DNA uptake and integration machinery is largely conserved.
source: While regulation of competence is highly diverse between naturally transformable bacteria, the actual DNA uptake and integration machinery is largely conserved (Chen and Dubnau, 2004; Johnston et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Chen and Dubnau, 2004; Johnston et al., 2014).

claim: During pneumococcal competence, exogenous double stranded DNA is bound by a type IV-like pilus and subsequently sequestered to the DNA uptake machinery.
source: During pneumococcal competence, exogenous double stranded DNA (dsDNA) is bound by a type IV-like pilus (Laurenceau et al., 2013) and subsequently sequestered to the DNA uptake machinery (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Laurenceau et al., 2013) and reference to Figure 1.

claim: In contrast to some other competent bacteria, pneumococcus binds and takes up DNA of any sequence, including non-kin DNA.
source: Note that in contrast to some other competent bacteria, pneumococcus binds and takes up DNA of any sequence, including non-kin DNA (Mell and Redfield, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Mell and Redfield, 2014).

claim: The dsDNA is processed into single-stranded DNA by the EndA nuclease and internalized through a membrane pore consisting of ComEC.
source: Next, the dsDNA is processed into single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) by the EndA nuclease and internalized through a membrane pore consisting of ComEC.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of the DNA uptake mechanism.

claim: Once inside, the ssDNA is bound by a competence-specific ssDNA-binding protein, SsbB, and stabilized by DprA and RecA.
source: Once inside, the ssDNA is bound by a competence-specific ssDNA-binding protein, SsbB, and stabilized by DprA and RecA (Attaiech et al., 2011; Bergé et al., 2003; Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Attaiech et al., 2011; Bergé et al., 2003) and reference to Figure 1.

claim: The ssDNA-protein complex undergoes homology scanning and forms a temporal hetero-duplex during strand invasion which can lead to homologous recombination.
source: This complex undergoes homology scanning and forms a temporal hetero-duplex during strand invasion which can lead to homologous recombination (Mortier-Barrière et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Mortier-Barrière et al., 2007).

claim: The competent transformation state in S. pneumoniae is transient as DprA interacts with phosphorylated ComE to inhibit its activity.
source: The competent transformation state in S. pneumoniae is transient as DprA interacts with phosphorylated ComE to inhibit its activity (Mirouze et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Mirouze et al., 2013).

claim: Several key Com proteins are rapidly turned over after their synthesis, leading to a window of DNA uptake of approximately 15 min.
source: In addition, several key Com proteins are rapidly turned over after their synthesis, leading to a window of DNA uptake of approximately 15 min (Liu et al., 2019; Tomasz, 1966; Weng et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Liu et al., 2019; Tomasz, 1966; Weng et al., 2013).

claim: Competence development in B. subtilis is limited to approximately 10% of the population.
source: While competence development in B. subtilis is limited to approximately 10% of the population (Maamar and Dubnau, 2005; Smits et al., 2005), up to 100% of cells within pneumococcal populations have been reported to become competent when induced with exogenously added synthetic CSP or when grown on semi-solid surfaces (Bergé et al., 2017; Domenech et al., 2018; Litt et al., 1958; Martin et al., 2010; Moreno-Gámez et al., 2017; Slager et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Maamar and Dubnau, 2005; Smits et al., 2005).

claim: Up to 100% of cells within pneumococcal populations have been reported to become competent when induced with exogenously added synthetic CSP or when grown on semi-solid surfaces.
source: While competence development in B. subtilis is limited to approximately 10% of the population (Maamar and Dubnau, 2005; Smits et al., 2005), up to 100% of cells within pneumococcal populations have been reported to become competent when induced with exogenously added synthetic CSP or when grown on semi-solid surfaces (Bergé et al., 2017; Domenech et al., 2018; Litt et al., 1958; Martin et al., 2010; Moreno-Gámez et al., 2017; Slager et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bergé et al., 2017; Domenech et al., 2018; Litt et al., 1958; Martin et al., 2010; Moreno-Gámez et al., 2017; Slager et al., 2014).

claim: In the presence of added CSP, the population rapidly activates ssbB.
source: As expected, under these experimental conditions, the population rapidly activates ssbB in the presence of added CSP, while in the absence of externally added CSP, the ssbB promoter peaks after approximately 100 min (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the absence of externally added CSP, the ssbB promoter peaks after approximately 100 min.
source: As expected, under these experimental conditions, the population rapidly activates ssbB in the presence of added CSP, while in the absence of externally added CSP, the ssbB promoter peaks after approximately 100 min (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Approximately 97% of the population was positive for ssbB expression 20 min after addition of synthetic CSP.
source: As shown in Figure 2B–C,~97% of the population was positive for ssbB expression 20 min after addition of synthetic CSP as determined by fluorescence microscopy followed by automated image analysis (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Spontaneous competence without the addition of synthetic CSP was reached in 92% of the population.
source: Importantly, spontaneous competence without the addition of synthetic CSP was reached in 92% of the population showing that almost all pneumococci, regardless of their cell length and cell-cycle status become naturally competent (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Almost all pneumococci, regardless of their cell length and cell-cycle status become naturally competent.
source: Importantly, spontaneous competence without the addition of synthetic CSP was reached in 92% of the population showing that almost all pneumococci, regardless of their cell length and cell-cycle status become naturally competent (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: msfYFP-ComEA, ComFA-msfYFP, and ComGA-msfYFP were expressed in the majority of the cells (~92, ~99, and ~99%, respectively) after 20 min of incubation with synthetic CSP.
source: In line with the fraction of cells that become competent, msfYFP-ComEA, ComFA-msfYFP, and ComGA-msfYFP were also expressed in the majority of the cells (~92,~99, and~99%, respectively) (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: All competent cells produce the DNA uptake machinery.
source: A double-labeled strain (strain OVL2536: PssbB-mScarlet-I, ComGA-msfYFP) demonstrated that all competent cells indeed produce the DNA uptake machinery (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: RecA and DprA were induced in most competent cells.
source: Similar to the DNA-uptake proteins, RecA and DprA were induced in most competent cells (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Approximately 90% of the population bound extracellular DNA after induction of competence with synthetic CSP in cells mutated for EndA.
source: After induction of competence with synthetic CSP of cells mutated for EndA (to prevent degradation of the exogenous DNA),~90% of the population bound extracellular DNA as visualized by fluorescence microscopy (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Without additional CSP, spontaneous competence led to most cells (89.6%) binding exogenous DNA.
source: Even without additional CSP, spontaneous competence also led to most cells (89.6%) binding exogenous DNA (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: In the encapsulated serotype 2 D39V strain, DNA mainly bound to the mid-cell positions of the cell, corresponding to the localization of the DNA uptake machinery particularly the ComEA receptor.
source: As observed before in an unencapsulated R6 strain (Bergé et al., 2013), we note that also in the encapsulated serotype 2 D39V strain, DNA mainly bound to the mid-cell positions of the cell, corresponding to the localization of the DNA uptake machinery particularly the ComEA receptor (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Bergé et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and by citation to published literature (Bergé et al., 2013).

claim: Pneumococcal competence development, the subsequent production of the DNA uptake and integration machinery, as well as DNA binding is highly efficient and occurs in nearly every cell of the population regardless of their cell-cycle state.
source: Collectively, these data validate by direct single-cell observations that pneumococcal competence development, the subsequent production of the DNA uptake and integration machinery, as well as DNA binding is highly efficient and occurs in nearly every cell of the population regardless of their cell-cycle state.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 2 and related supplements.

claim: Traditional transformation efficiency evaluation methods using antibiotic selection can lead to overestimation of transformation efficiencies due to inefficient separation of transformed from non-transformed daughter cells and nongenetic inheritance of antibiotic resistance.
source: Traditionally, transformation efficiencies are evaluated using antibiotic selection methods. However, these selection methods have limitations because they depend on the counting of colony forming units, which can lead to the overestimation of transformation efficiencies, due to inefficient separation of transformed from non-transformed daughter cells and nongenetic inheritance of antibiotic resistance (Dalia and Dalia, 2019; Domenech et al., 2018; Ephrussi-Taylor, 1962; Ephrussi-Taylor, 1958; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dalia and Dalia, 2019; Domenech et al., 2018; Ephrussi-Taylor, 1962; Ephrussi-Taylor, 1958) and reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Successfully transformed recipient cells will produce functional HlpA-mScarlet-I that can be quantified by fluorescence microscopy or flow cytometry upon uptake, integration and expression of exogenous transforming DNA containing the donor construct.
source: Upon uptake, integration and expression of exogenous transforming DNA (tDNA) containing the donor construct (intact hlpA-mScarlet-I), successfully transformed recipient cells will produce functional HlpA-mScarlet-I that can be quantified by fluorescence microscopy or flow cytometry (Figure 3B and C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B, 3C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The fluorescence reporter system does not affect growth regardless of the presence of the stop codon.
source: Note that this reporter system does not affect growth regardless of the presence of the stop codon (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and that flow-cytometry analysis slightly overestimates the real transformation efficiencies due to cell chaining (Figure 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4, see below).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Flow-cytometry analysis slightly overestimates the real transformation efficiencies due to cell chaining.
source: Note that this reporter system does not affect growth regardless of the presence of the stop codon (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and that flow-cytometry analysis slightly overestimates the real transformation efficiencies due to cell chaining (Figure 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4, see below).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The initial recipient cell expresses HlpA-mScarlet-I right after the addition of tDNA before the first cell division as red fluorescent signals above background levels can be detected.
source: When quantifying the fluorescence signals and superimposing this on a cell lineage tree constructed using a set of new scripts written in BactMAP (van Raaphorst et al., 2020) (see Materials and methods), it becomes apparent that the initial recipient cell already expresses HlpA-mScarlet-I right after the addition of tDNA before the first cell division as red fluorescent signals above background levels can be detected (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Only half of the recipients' descendants appear to strongly express HlpA-mScarlet-I.
source: Notably, only half of the recipients' descendants appear to strongly express HlpA-mScarlet-I (Figure 3E, right lineage).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: After three more divisions the non-transformed lineage no longer expresses red fluorescence.
source: Contrary, after three more divisions the non-transformed lineage no longer expresses red fluorescence (Figure 3E, left lineage).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: There is a period of nongenetic inheritance in daughter cells during transformation.
source: These results are in line with a recent study in Vibrio cholerae that showed a period of nongenetic inheritance in daughter cells during transformation (Dalia and Dalia, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Dalia and Dalia, 2019) and by inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Recombination occurs by direct integration of the ssDNA donor and forms a hetero-duplex.
source: In line with current models of transformation (Davidoff-Abelson and Dubnau, 1971; Ephrussi-Taylor and Gray, 1966; Fox and Allen, 1964; Gabor and Hotchkiss, 1966; Lacks, 1962; Méjean and Claverys, 1984; Piechowska and Fox, 1971), these observations are consistent with a model in which recombination occurs by direct integration of the ssDNA donor and forms a hetero-duplex.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Davidoff-Abelson and Dubnau, 1971; Ephrussi-Taylor and Gray, 1966; Fox and Allen, 1964; Gabor and Hotchkiss, 1966; Lacks, 1962; Méjean and Claverys, 1984; Piechowska and Fox, 1971) and by inference from the experimental observations.

claim: At least one round of DNA replication and division is required to generate two different homo-duplex chromosomes in progeny cells.
source: Therefore, at least one round of DNA replication and division is required to generate two different homo-duplex chromosomes in progeny cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations and reference to Figure 3F.

claim: Phenotypic expression derived from the acquired allele might occur prior to forming a homo-duplex if the transformed ssDNA replaced the anti-sense, noncoding strand.
source: The fact that we initially also observe fluorescence in the untransformed lineage suggests that phenotypic expression derived from the acquired allele might occur prior to forming a homo-duplex. In this case, the transformed ssDNA likely replaced the anti-sense, noncoding strand so functional hlpA-mScarlet-I could be immediately transcribed after integration via RecA-directed homeologous recombination (mismatched pairing between exchanged DNA strands that are tolerated during the process of homologous recombination).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Phenotypic expression in cells can occur if the transformed locus gets replicated, resulting in two homo-duplexes (transformed and original allele), and then transcribed before division of the cell.
source: Alternatively, phenotypic expression in these cells can occur if the transformed locus gets replicated, resulting in two homo-duplexes (transformed and original allele), and then transcribed before division of the cell (Dalia and Dalia, 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations and supported by a citation to published literature (Dalia and Dalia, 2019).

claim: Higher transformation frequencies were observed at higher donor DNA concentrations and with longer homology regions.
source: In line with studies using classical plating methods to assess transformation efficiencies (Keller et al., 2019; Lee et al., 1998), higher transformation frequencies were observed at higher donor DNA concentrations and with longer homology regions (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B and citations to published literature (Keller et al., 2019; Lee et al., 1998).

claim: The frequency of transformation plateaued at ~50% regardless of the concentration of donor DNA and sequence homology length.
source: Interestingly, the frequency of transformation plateaued at ~50% regardless of the concentration of donor DNA and sequence homology length (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Transformation frequencies of higher than 75% and up to 100% have been reported using traditional plating assays.
source: This is in contrast to reported transformation frequencies using traditional plating assays where transformation frequencies of higher than 75% (Ephrussi-Taylor, 1958) and up to 100% (Marie et al., 2017) have been reported.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ephrussi-Taylor, 1958; Marie et al., 2017).

claim: The discrepancy in transformation frequencies between single-cell assays and traditional plating assays can be explained by the lack of separation of transformed from non-transformed cells within the counted colony.
source: This discrepancy can be explained by the lack of separation of transformed from non-transformed cells within the counted colony (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations and reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The spv_1159-sfGFP-based transformation reporter demonstrated similar transformation characteristics as the hlpA-mScarlet-I reporter in time-lapse microscopy and flow-cytometry analysis.
source: Indeed, this spv_1159-sfGFP-based transformation reporter demonstrated similar transformation characteristics as the hlpA-mScarlet-I reporter in time-lapse microscopy and flow-cytometry analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Video 3.

claim: The transformation frequency of the spv_1159-sfGFP reporter was dependent on donor DNA concentration and never exceeded ~50%.
source: The transformation frequency of the spv_1159-sfGFP reporter was also dependent on donor DNA concentration and never exceeded ~50% (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There is a limit on the maximum efficiency of transformation, despite the fact that most cells become competent and bind extracellular DNA.
source: These data show that there is a limit on the maximum efficiency of transformation, despite the fact that most cells become competent and bind extracellular DNA (Figure 2) and support a model in which in general only one of the recipient allele strands is replaced by the donor DNA (Ephrussi-Taylor, 1966; Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3F, and supported by a citation to published literature (Ephrussi-Taylor, 1966).

claim: In general only one of the recipient allele strands is replaced by the donor DNA during transformation.
source: These data show that there is a limit on the maximum efficiency of transformation, despite the fact that most cells become competent and bind extracellular DNA (Figure 2) and support a model in which in general only one of the recipient allele strands is replaced by the donor DNA (Ephrussi-Taylor, 1966; Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3F, and supported by a citation to published literature (Ephrussi-Taylor, 1966).

claim: During competence-dependent transformation, given the donor DNA is of sufficient length and concentration, in principle all targeted loci can be replaced at least on one strand.
source: Importantly, these experiments indicate that during competence-dependent transformation, given the donor DNA is of sufficient (homology) length and concentration (see Discussion), in principle all targeted loci can be replaced at least on one strand.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: hexA does not play a significant role in the fluorescence-based transformation reporter system.
source: To test whether hexA plays a role in our reporter system, we quantified transformation efficiencies in a hexA mutant background. This showed no significant recombination differences compared to the wild-type background (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The fluorescence-based transformation assay depends on the competence-induced homologous recombinase, RecA.
source: To test if our transformation reporter system depends on the competence-induced homologous recombinase, RecA, we depleted RecA expression level using CRISPR interference (Liu et al., 2017; Figure 5D). In control strain VL3485 (Plac_dcas9, without sgRNA), induction of dCas9 by IPTG did not affect the transformation efficiency with hlpA-mScarlet-I tDNA. However, when RecA expression was depleted by induction with IPTG in strain VL3486 (Plac_dcas9+sgRNA-recA), the transformation frequency was decreased in an IPTG-dose dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D and citation to published literature (Liu et al., 2017).

claim: When RecA expression was depleted by induction with IPTG, the transformation frequency was decreased in an IPTG-dose dependent manner.
source: However, when RecA expression was depleted by induction with IPTG in strain VL3486 (Plac_dcas9+sgRNA-recA), the transformation frequency was decreased in an IPTG-dose dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The CRISPRi depletion levels of RecA during competence did not affect bacterial growth.
source: Note that although RecA is known to be critical for optimal growth in S. pneumoniae (Mortier-Barrière et al., 1998), the CRISPRi depletion levels during competence did not affect bacterial growth (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and citation to published literature (Mortier-Barrière et al., 1998).

claim: The fluorescence-based transformation assay faithfully reflects RecA-dependent homeologous recombination events.
source: Collectively, these data show that our fluorescence-based transformation assay faithfully reflects RecA-dependent homeologous recombination events.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Transformation efficiencies were of a similar order across all tested loci and genetic orientations, with a maximal recombination efficiency of approximately 50%.
source: As shown in Figure 4, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, transformation efficiencies were of a similar order across all tested loci and genetic orientations, with a maximal recombination efficiency of approximately 50%.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Certain loci consistently demonstrate higher transformation efficiencies than others.
source: We do note that certain loci consistently demonstrate higher transformation efficiencies than others (cf. CEP locus vs bgaA locus, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), but no significant differences were observed regarding the orientation of the construct (see Discussion).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant differences in transformation efficiency were observed regarding the orientation of the construct.
source: We do note that certain loci consistently demonstrate higher transformation efficiencies than others (cf. CEP locus vs bgaA locus, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), but no significant differences were observed regarding the orientation of the construct (see Discussion).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Transformants rapidly expressing HlpA-mScarlet-I are possible noncoding strand or double stranded recombinants.
source: Indeed, we can observe all different scenarios with transformants rapidly expressing HlpA-mScarlet-I (possible noncoding strand or double stranded recombinants) and cells that only express HlpA-mScarlet-I after the first cell division (possible coding strand recombinants) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C, Video 4).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and Video 4.

claim: Cells that only express HlpA-mScarlet-I after the first cell division are possible coding strand recombinants.
source: Indeed, we can observe all different scenarios with transformants rapidly expressing HlpA-mScarlet-I (possible noncoding strand or double stranded recombinants) and cells that only express HlpA-mScarlet-I after the first cell division (possible coding strand recombinants) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C, Video 4).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and Video 4.

claim: There is no preference for integration at either the leading or lagging strand during transformation.
source: Together with the 'bulk' (FACS) single-cell transformation experiments described above, the time-lapse data strongly suggest that there is no preference for integration at either the leading or lagging strand and that this is an unbiased event.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Either strand of the incoming dsDNA is degraded randomly by EndA and either strand has a similar chance of being integrated.
source: These findings correspond with work done in the 1960s and 1970s that showed that either strand of the incoming dsDNA is degraded randomly by EndA and either strand has a similar chance of being integrated (Puyet et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Puyet et al., 1990).

claim: 7% of transformation events in V. cholerae occurred at both strands of the integration site.
source: Recent work in V. cholerae demonstrated that 7% of transformation events occurred at both strands of the integration site, and it was speculated that this was because of integration of multiple donor ssDNA's replacing both the leading and lagging strand of the recipient.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from published literature.

claim: By recording 76 single-cell transformation events using time-lapse microscopy, six cases (7.8%) were found in which both daughter cells expressed fluorescence, suggestive of double transformation events on both strands.
source: By recording 76 single-cell transformation events using time-lapse microscopy, we found six cases in which both daughter cells (7.8%) expressed fluorescence, suggestive of double transformation events on both strands.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from time-lapse microscopy.

claim: Hetero-duplex DNA can be transcribed by RNAP and do not necessarily require a round of DNA replication to form homo-duplex DNA.
source: These findings also indirectly indicate that hetero-duplex DNA can be transcribed by RNAP and do not necessarily require a round of DNA replication to form homo-duplex DNA (see below and [Uptain and Chamberlin, 1997]).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations and supported by a citation to published literature (Uptain and Chamberlin, 1997).

claim: Hetero-duplexes with exogenous DNA are made across all available loci regardless of reading strand or distance to oriC.
source: Together, these data show that hetero-duplexes with exogenous DNA are made across all available loci regardless of reading strand or distance to oriC.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Under ideal conditions with long flanking homology regions and high DNA concentrations, all available recombination sites are transformed on at least one of the strands.
source: The previous experiments demonstrated that, under ideal conditions with long flanking homology regions and high DNA concentrations, all available recombination sites are transformed on at least one of the strands.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Pneumococcal natural transformation is capable to deal with multiple donor DNAs for genetic recombination.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that pneumococcal natural transformation is capable to deal with multiple donor DNAs for genetic recombination (Dalia et al., 2014; Lam et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dalia et al., 2014; Lam et al., 2020).

claim: The DNA uptake and recombination process in S. pneumoniae is complete within 15 min.
source: Also, it has been reported that the DNA uptake and recombination process in S. pneumoniae is complete within 15 min (Bergé et al., 2003), which is a shorter time window than the doubling time (Ephrussi-Taylor, 1966).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bergé et al., 2003; Ephrussi-Taylor, 1966).

claim: Transformation efficiencies of the dual reporter strain with each single donor DNA at the saturated concentration typically reached 50% for both hlpA-mScarlet-I and spv_1159-sfGFP.
source: Transformation efficiencies of this reporter strain with each single donor DNA at the saturated concentration typically reached 50% for both hlpA-mScarlet-I and spv_1159-sfGFP as quantified by microscopy (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: When both donor DNAs were provided, double transformants were observed (15.6 ± 4.4%) as well as single hlpA-mScarlet-I transformants (20.2 ± 8.9%) and single spv_1159-sfGFP transformants (15.2 ± 4.9%).
source: When both donor DNAs were provided, double transformants were observed (15.6 ± 4.4%) as well as single hlpA-mScarlet-I transformants (20.2 ± 8.9%) and single spv_1159-sfGFP transformants (15.2 ± 4.9%).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Single recipients could successfully recombine both fragments during time-lapse imaging.
source: Time-lapse imaging of competent recipient VL1803 cells with both donor DNAs clearly demonstrated that single recipients could successfully recombine both fragments (Figure 6B and C, Videos 5,6).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B, 6C, and Videos 5 and 6.

claim: On average, the fraction of non-transformed cells is close to 50% (48.9 ± 9.5%) when multiple donor DNAs are provided.
source: We note that, on average, the fraction of non-transformed cells is close to 50% (48.9 ± 9.5%), implying that each recombination event is not independent from the next or that there is an upper limit to the number of successful recombinations, otherwise we would expect the fraction of non-transformed cells to decrease with multiple donor DNAs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data and inference from Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Each recombination event is not independent from the next or there is an upper limit to the number of successful recombinations.
source: We note that, on average, the fraction of non-transformed cells is close to 50% (48.9 ± 9.5%), implying that each recombination event is not independent from the next or that there is an upper limit to the number of successful recombinations, otherwise we would expect the fraction of non-transformed cells to decrease with multiple donor DNAs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Each recombination event is independent from the next but due to recombination events outside the stop codon SNP, which cannot be quantified in the setup, a reduced transformation efficiency is recorded.
source: An alternative model could be that each recombination event is independent from the next but due to recombination events outside the stop codon SNP, which cannot be quantified in our setup, a reduced transformation efficiency is recorded (see Discussion).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about an alternative model.

claim: Every possible recombination event happened within the population when transforming with three tDNAs: cells with just a single recombination event, two recombination events, or even three recombination events.
source: Interestingly, every possible recombination event happened within the population: cells were observed in which just a single recombination event took place (the most occurring type of transformation), two recombination events (2.2 ± 0.9%, 4.1 ± 2.7% or 2.1 ± 1.8% for each possible combination) or even three recombination events (1.5 ± 1.1% of all cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: More than half of the population (58.7 ± 13.4%) did not show any fluorescence when simultaneously transformed with three tDNAs.
source: Nevertheless, more than half of the population (58.7 ± 13.4%) did not show any fluorescence when simultaneously transformed with three tDNAs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Each transformation is in principle independent from the next.
source: These observations support a model in which each transformation is in principle independent from the next (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Co-transformation of strain VL1803 with E. coli DNA significantly reduced the transformation efficiency.
source: Indeed, as shown in Figure 7E, co-transformation of strain VL1803 (hlpA-stop-mScarlet-I, spv_1159-stop-sfGFP) with E. coli DNA significantly reduced the transformation efficiency.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: When 0.32 μM of hlpA-mScarlet-I tDNA alone was used as 7 kb donor DNA, approximately 43% of cells were transformed.
source: When 0.32 μM of hlpA-mScarlet-I tDNA alone was used as 7 kb donor DNA, approximately 43% of cells were transformed.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: When 0.32 μM of hlpA-mScarlet-I tDNA was given in the presence of saturating amounts of E. coli DNA (3.2 μM), only 3% of transformants were observed.
source: However, when 0.32 μM of hlpA-mScarlet-I tDNA was given in the presence of saturating amounts of E. coli DNA (3.2 μM), only 3% of transformants were observed.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The fact that transformation efficiencies never reach higher than 50% of the population even in the presence of multiple tDNAs is because of saturation of the DNA uptake and integration machinery.
source: Together, these data suggest that the fact that we never reach transformation efficiencies higher than 50% of the population even in the presence of multiple tDNAs, is because of saturation of the DNA uptake and integration machinery.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: The saturation of the DNA uptake and integration machinery can be caused by non-successful recombination events with donor DNA or successful recombination events with the donor DNA but outside of the stop SNP that cannot be detected in the single-cell assay.
source: The saturation can be caused by non-successful recombination events with donor DNA or successful recombination events with the donor DNA but outside of the stop SNP that cannot be detected in the single-cell assay (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In pneumococcal biofilms, competence and fratricide are strongly induced, resulting in high relative concentrations of DNA.
source: Indeed, in pneumococcal biofilms, which are a model for nasopharyngeal colonization, competence and fratricide are strongly induced, resulting in high relative concentrations of DNA.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge.

claim: In the co-culture system, single transformation efficiency with smR or novR was 5.70 × 10−2% (SD, 5.70 × 10−2%) or 1.75 × 10−2% (SD, 1.68 × 10−2%), respectively.
source: As shown in Figure 8B, also in this more realistic model, very high transformation efficiencies are obtained with a single transformation efficiency with smR or novR of 5.70 × 10−2% (SD, 5.70 × 10−2%) or 1.75 × 10−2% (SD, 1.68 × 10−2%), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Double transformation efficiency with both smR and novR was 8.01 × 10−5% (SD, 9.92 × 10−5%), which is close to the product of the single transformation efficiencies.
source: Double transformation efficiency with both smR and novR was 8.01 × 10−5% (SD, 9.92 × 10−5%), which is close to the product of the single transformation efficiencies (5.70 × 10−2% × 1.75×10−2% = 9.9×10−4%).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Using strain R4574 as donor (same genotype as R4692, but not harboring smR or novR allele) never generated streptomycin nor novobiocin-resistant R895, demonstrating that de novo mutations conferring resistance do not occur in this experimental setup.
source: As a control, we also performed experiments using strain R4574 as donor (same genotype as R4692, but not harboring smR or novR allele), which never generated streptomycin nor novobiocin-resistant R895, demonstrating that de novo mutations conferring resistance do not occur in this experimental setup.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Multiple transformation events occur efficiently and independently even in more realistic settings within sessile co-cultures.
source: Together, these experiments support our single- cell observations that multiple transformation events occur efficiently and independently even in more realistic settings within sessile co-cultures.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: The species of S. pneumoniae is vastly diverse with a core genome of approximately 500–1100 orthologues genes and a pan-genome of 5000–7000 orthologs.
source: The species of S. pneumoniae is vastly diverse with a core genome of approximately 500–1100 orthologues genes and a pan-genome of 5000–7000 orthologs (Hiller and Sá-Leão, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Hiller and Sá-Leão, 2018).

claim: Many genes in S. pneumoniae are mosaic such as several genes encoding for penicillin-binding proteins in penicillin-resistant clinical strains.
source: In addition, many genes are mosaic such as several genes encoding for penicillin-binding proteins in penicillin-resistant clinical strains (Hakenbeck et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Hakenbeck et al., 2012).

claim: One of the main reasons for the high level of genome plasticity and rapidly changing population dynamics is the highly conserved competence-based transformation system present in nearly all pneumococcal genomes.
source: One of the main reasons for the high level of genome plasticity and rapidly changing population dynamics is because of the highly conserved competence-based transformation system present in nearly all pneumococcal genomes (Croucher et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Croucher et al., 2016).

claim: Rapid spread of antibiotic resistance alleles and capsule loci have been observed among human populations under selective pressure.
source: Indeed, rapid spread of antibiotic resistance alleles and capsule loci have been observed among human populations under selective pressure (Chewapreecha et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Chewapreecha et al., 2014).

claim: The uptake, integration, and expression of tDNA are highly efficient and are largely independent from the recipient's cell-cycle stage or of the chromosomal position of the target locus.
source: Here, we investigated the molecular basis for competence-dependent transformation at the single-cell level and show that the uptake, integration, and expression of tDNA are highly efficient and are largely independent from the recipient's cell-cycle stage or of the chromosomal position of the target locus.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The recombination of three different tDNAs in single recipient cells was visualized and quantified, demonstrating the efficiency of the pneumococcal transformation process.
source: Indeed, using the system developed here, we could visualize and quantify the recombination of three different tDNAs in single recipient cells demonstrating the efficiency of the pneumococcal transformation process.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Genome sequencing has indicated that up to 29 recombination events may have taken place in a single round of transformation in the same cell when selecting for the transfer of an antibiotic resistance allele in S. pneumoniae.
source: Genome sequencing has indicated that up to 29 recombination events may have taken place in a single round of transformation in the same cell when selecting for the transfer of an antibiotic resistance allele in S. pneumoniae (Cowley et al., 2018), while 40 recombination events have been reported in B. subtilis (Carrasco et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Cowley et al., 2018; Carrasco et al., 2016).

claim: 40 recombination events have been reported in B. subtilis during transformation.
source: Genome sequencing has indicated that up to 29 recombination events may have taken place in a single round of transformation in the same cell when selecting for the transfer of an antibiotic resistance allele in S. pneumoniae (Cowley et al., 2018), while 40 recombination events have been reported in B. subtilis (Carrasco et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Carrasco et al., 2016).

claim: Multiple recombination events are not an anomaly and are possible during a single transformation episode, even in the absence of selection.
source: Our work now provides direct evidence that this is not an anomaly and that multiple recombination events are possible during a single transformation episode, even in the absence of selection.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Typically only one recipient strand is replaced during competence-dependent transformation.
source: Besides shedding light on the efficiency by which transformation can happen in S. pneumoniae, by imaging transformation at the single-cell level, we provide direct evidence that typically only one recipient strand is replaced during competence-dependent transformation, and that there is no bias toward replacement of the leading or lagging strand.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: In approximately 7% of transformants, both strands can be replaced, which is likely caused by DNA repair leading to removal of the recipient strand on the hetero-duplex or by integration of multiple tDNAs.
source: As observed in V. cholerae, in approximately 7% of transformants, both strands can be replaced, which is likely caused by DNA repair leading to removal of the recipient strand on the hetero-duplex or by integration of multiple tDNAs (Dalia and Dalia, 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and supported by a citation to published literature (Dalia and Dalia, 2019).

claim: The replaced noncoding strand by recombination within the hetero-duplex is immediately transcribed by RNAP and can lead to lineages of cells with nongenetic inherited phenotypes.
source: In addition, our single-cell observations suggest that the replaced noncoding strand by recombination within the hetero-duplex is immediately transcribed by RNAP and can lead to lineages of cells with nongenetic inherited phenotypes, or that the transformed allele is replicated and transcribed well before cell division occurs (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations shown in Figure 3.

claim: The transformed allele is replicated and transcribed well before cell division occurs.
source: In addition, our single-cell observations suggest that the replaced noncoding strand by recombination within the hetero-duplex is immediately transcribed by RNAP and can lead to lineages of cells with nongenetic inherited phenotypes, or that the transformed allele is replicated and transcribed well before cell division occurs (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations shown in Figure 3.

claim: Any site regardless of its chromosomal position or orientation with regard to DNA replication can be efficiently transformed, although not with the exact same efficiencies.
source: We show that any site regardless of its chromosomal position or orientation with regard to DNA replication can be efficiently transformed, although not with the exact same efficiencies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Possible explanations for local difference in recombination efficiency could be the levels of DNA compaction or transcription activity.
source: Possible explanations for local difference in recombination efficiency could be the levels of DNA compaction or transcription activity.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation.

claim: RecA-mediated DNA strand exchange is a reversible reaction in vitro.
source: As RecA-mediated DNA strand exchange is a reversible reaction in vitro (Dutreix et al., 1991; Konforti and Davis, 1990), under steady state conditions DNA strand exchange rarely reaches 50% efficiency.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dutreix et al., 1991; Konforti and Davis, 1990).

claim: Under steady state conditions DNA strand exchange rarely reaches 50% efficiency in vitro.
source: As RecA-mediated DNA strand exchange is a reversible reaction in vitro (Dutreix et al., 1991; Konforti and Davis, 1990), under steady state conditions DNA strand exchange rarely reaches 50% efficiency.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dutreix et al., 1991; Konforti and Davis, 1990).

claim: In vivo, when providing a single tDNA to competent cells, 50% DNA strand exchange is readily reached, highlighting that this process is highly efficient under experimental conditions.
source: However, in vivo, when providing a single tDNA to competent cells, we readily reach 50% DNA strand exchange, again highlighting that this process is highly efficient under our experimental conditions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: The percentage of untransformed cells is lower when three tDNAs are provided instead of two tDNAs (~58% vs ~49% of untransformed cells, respectively).
source: Interestingly, we find that the percentage of untransformed cells is lower when three tDNAs are provided instead of two tDNAs (~58% vs ~49% of untransformed cells, respectively: Figures 6 and 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: In principle, every recombination event is independent of the next, but many unsuccessful recombination events and successful recombination events outside the stop codon of the reporter are taking place and this limits the efficiency of site-specific recombination.
source: Together with the observation that the presence of non-homologous DNA reduced our observed transformation efficiency (Figure 7E), suggests that, in principle, every recombination event is independent of the next, but that many unsuccessful recombination events and successful recombination events outside the stop codon of our reporter are taking place and that this limits the efficiency of site-specific recombination (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 7E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, and Figure 7F.

claim: The limitation on competence-dependent transformation ensures that in most cases one copy of the original recipient DNA remains unaltered.
source: The overall biological implication of the limitation on competence-dependent transformation is that this mechanism ensures that in most cases one copy of the original recipient DNA remains unaltered.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: The limitation on competence-dependent transformation might represent a fail-safe scenario so that in case a deleterious tDNA is incorporated, at least one daughter cell will survive.
source: This might represent a fail-safe scenario so that in case a deleterious tDNA is incorporated, at least one daughter cell will survive.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation.

claim: Being able to safely sample from a large pan-genome might contribute to the vast genome plasticity and genome diversity as observed in natural pneumococcal populations.
source: While this might be considered as a 'spandrel' effect: a characteristic that flows inevitably from a selected phenotype but has not been selected for directly (Gould and Lewontin, 1979), being able to safely sample from a large pan-genome might contribute to the vast genome plasticity and genome diversity as observed in natural pneumococcal populations.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and supported by a citation to published literature (Gould and Lewontin, 1979).

claim: Highly efficient HGT and independent transfer of genetic markers between a donor and recipient pneumococcal strain growing together on agar plates was observed.
source: Interestingly, we also find highly efficient HGT and independent transfer of genetic markers between a donor and recipient pneumococcal strain growing together on agar plates (Figure 8), indicating that our single-cell observations under laboratory conditions also reflect settings that depend on lysis of the donor cell and uptake of chromosomal DNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Single-cell observations under laboratory conditions reflect settings that depend on lysis of the donor cell and uptake of chromosomal DNA.
source: Interestingly, we also find highly efficient HGT and independent transfer of genetic markers between a donor and recipient pneumococcal strain growing together on agar plates (Figure 8), indicating that our single-cell observations under laboratory conditions also reflect settings that depend on lysis of the donor cell and uptake of chromosomal DNA.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Within isogenic populations, all cells become naturally competent and bind exogenous DNA.
source: We show that within isogenic populations, all cells become naturally competent and bind exogenous DNA.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Transformation is highly efficient and the chromosomal location of the integration site or whether the transformed gene is encoded on the leading or lagging strand has limited influence on recombination efficiency.
source: We find that transformation is highly efficient and that the chromosomal location of the integration site or whether the transformed gene is encoded on the leading or lagging strand has limited influence on recombination efficiency.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Multiple recombination events in single recipients have been observed in real-time.
source: Indeed, we have observed multiple recombination events in single recipients in real-time.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from time-lapse microscopy.

claim: Because of saturation and because a single-stranded donor DNA replaces the original allele, transformation efficiency has an upper threshold of approximately 50% of the population.
source: However, because of saturation and because a single-stranded donor DNA replaces the original allele, transformation efficiency has an upper threshold of approximately 50% of the population.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: The fixed mechanism of transformation results in a fail-safe strategy for the population as half of the population generally keeps an intact copy of the original genome.
source: The fixed mechanism of transformation results in a fail-safe strategy for the population as half of the population generally keeps an intact copy of the original genome.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.
